audience.programmeDescription: Dutch Language and Culture at Radboud studies Dutch and Flemish literature, the structure and history of Dutch, and the use of language in communication. It combines textual analysis, literary and linguistic research methods, and independent research.
audience.comparisonExplanation: A complete UCR comparison is withheld while Radboud’s current curriculum needs clarification. The same Psycholinguistics course appears in two years, leaving 5 EC without a verified distinct allocation. Related UCR literature, rhetoric and language research are useful foundations, but complete UCR programmes are not approved here.

First-year mentoring and the Dutch academic-language diagnostic, plus second-year mentoring and personal development, add no credits. Attendance applies to mentoring and first-year courses.

provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Personal & Professional Development
provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.text: History of Empires examines empires across global history and competing theories of empire. Students study expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. Historical cases, source analysis and an independent research essay connect theoretical interpretation with specific imperial experiences.

provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Neurobiology
provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Neurobiology studies nervous systems and behaviour through comparative anatomy, evolution and physiology. Students examine animal behaviour, research models, welfare and research ethics, then connect biological rhythms and regulatory behaviour to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based report apply neurobiological concepts.

provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Higher Order Functions
provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Higher Order Functions deepens knowledge of neurophysiology, neuroanatomy and experimental cognitive neuroscience. Topics include attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness. An attentional-blink experiment and a team research proposal develop engagement with empirical research, experimental design and ethical reflection.

provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Psycholinguistics
provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.

provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models for group comparisons, categorical outcomes and latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports practical exercises; data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions to appropriate models, assumption checks and clear reporting.

provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics introduces systematic reviews and meta-analysis to synthesise results across studies. Students use R to conduct analyses, work with data structures and packages, estimate treatment effects and examine their consistency across studies. Presentations and active research tasks develop evidence-synthesis skills.

provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.

Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.

provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Dutch
provisionalSharedDescriptionReviews.text: This course aims to develop basic skills and strategies necessary to successfully handle uncomplicated oral and written communication in Dutch in a variety of social situations that you may encounter in daily life in the Netherlands. The emphasis in the course will be on speaking in Dutch in day-to-day situations on the one hand and understanding Dutch culture on the other hand. At the end of the course students can orally express and write about themselves in Dutch, who they are, describe their family background, and interact with others in a simple way.
